lead: Cut a stressed point on a plane tilted by angle θ and the normal stress changes while a shear appears. At two particular tilts the shear vanishes and the normal stress reaches its largest and smallest values for that point. Those are the principal planes, and the two normal stresses on them are the principal stresses. They tell a designer where a brittle part will crack and which plane a twisted shaft will fail on. This chapter finds them from σx, σy and τxy alone.
prereq: You need: 2.2 for the normal and shear stress on a tilted plane, 2.3 for the 2θ transformation, and calculus for locating a maximum.

blocks.text: Take a small element in plane stress. It carries normal stresses σx and σy in MPa, tension positive, and a shear τxy in MPa on the x and y faces. Three numbers describe the whole state at that point.

blocks.where: σn is the normal stress on a plane whose normal is at angle θ from the x axis, in MPa; σx, σy are the given normal stresses in MPa; τxy is the given shear in MPa; θ is measured anticlockwise from the x face.

blocks.text: The first term is a constant, the average of the given normal stresses. The rest is a cosine wave, so σn swings between a high and a low twice in every full turn of the plane. The shear on the same plane is also a wave in 2θ.

Ask where σn is extreme. There dσn/dθ = 0, and the shear then comes out zero as well. Those planes are the principal planes; the normal stresses on them are the principal stresses σ1 and σ2. Read them as two pure pulls or pushes at right angles, with no shear — the simplest description of the same stress state.
Differentiate σn with respect to θ and set the result to zero.

blocks.where: θp is the angle from the x face to a principal plane, in degrees or radians; the other symbols are as before.

blocks.text: This is the same condition as τ = 0, so principal planes and shear-free planes are one and the same. The tangent repeats every 180° in its argument, so 2θp has two solutions 180° apart. In θ that gives two principal planes 90° apart, for every stress state.
Put θp back into σn and simplify. Draw a right triangle with opposite side 2τxy and adjacent side σx − σy; sin2θp and cos2θp drop out and σn collapses to a centre plus or minus a radius.
C = (σx+σy)/2,  R = √(((σx−σy)/2)² + τxy²),  σ1 = C + R,  σ2 = C − R
blocks.where: C is the centre, the average normal stress, in MPa; R is the radius in MPa; σ1 is the algebraically larger principal stress and σ2 the smaller, both in MPa.

blocks.text: σ1 is the more tensile of the two, not the larger in size. Two checks catch most slips: σ1 + σ2 = σx + σy = 2C must hold, and the plane at θp carries σ1 while the plane at θp + 90° carries σ2.

sections.h3: Maximum shear and the third dimension

blocks.text: Shear on a tilted plane is τ = −((σx−σy)/2)sin2θ + τxy cos2θ. Its extreme value is the radius itself.

blocks.where: τmax is the largest in-plane shear stress in MPa; θs is the angle of the plane carrying it, measured from the x face.

blocks.text: The two answers sit 45° apart: θs = θp ± 45°. On the maximum-shear plane the normal stress is C, not zero. Pure torsion is the sharpest case: σ1 = +τ, σ2 = −τ, and the worst shear is τ on planes at 45° to the shaft axis.

In three dimensions a point has three principal stresses, ordered σ1 ≥ σ2 ≥ σ3, along three mutually perpendicular directions. In plane stress, on a free surface, one of the three is zero. Call that one the third stress; its rank comes from the ordering. If both in-plane stresses are tensile it ranks as σ3; if both are compressive it ranks as σ1. Each pair has its own maximum shear, and the largest of the three is the absolute maximum shear.

blocks.where: σ1, σ2, σ3 are the three principal stresses in MPa, ordered algebraically; τabs is the absolute maximum shear stress at the point, in MPa.

blocks.text: If σ1 and σ2 have opposite signs, the zero stress lies between them and τabs = R. If they have the same sign, τabs = max(|σ1|,|σ2|)/2, which is larger than R, so quoting R is wrong. Solving the full 3D cubic is asked in only a few universities; 2.5 gets the plane case faster by drawing.

figure.caption: The route from three given stresses to the principal stresses, the principal angle and the maximum in-plane shear. The shear answer is the radius, the same number that shifts the centre to σ1 and σ2.

spec.title: Principal stress route
spec.aria: A flow from given stresses to centre and radius, then to principal stresses and to principal angle with maximum shear.

examples.question: A point in plane stress has σx = 80 MPa, σy = −40 MPa and τxy = 50 MPa. Find the principal stresses, the principal plane angles, and the maximum in-plane shear stress. State whether that shear is also the absolute maximum shear.
steps: Check: σ1 + σ2 = 98.10 − 58.10 = 40 MPa, and σx + σy = 80 − 40 = 40 MPa; they match.
Second principal plane: θp + 90° = 109.90°, carrying σ2.
Maximum in-plane shear: τmax = R = 78.10 MPa, on a plane at θs = 19.90° − 45° = −25.10° from the x face.
Absolute maximum shear: the three principal stresses in order are 98.10, 0 and −58.10 MPa. The zero stress lies between the other two, so τabs = (98.10 − (−58.10))/2 = 78.10 MPa, equal to R.
examples.answer: σ1 = 98.10 MPa (tension), σ2 = −58.10 MPa (compression), θp = 19.90° and 109.90°, and τmax = 78.10 MPa in plane, which also equals the absolute maximum shear because the zero principal stress lies between the other two.
examples.check:
import math

sx, sy, txy = 80.0, -40.0, 50.0

C = (sx + sy) / 2
R = math.sqrt(((sx - sy) / 2) ** 2 + txy ** 2)
s1 = C + R
s2 = C - R
theta_p = 0.5 * math.degrees(math.atan2(2 * txy, sx - sy))
tmax = R

print(round(C, 2))
print(round(R, 2))
print(round(s1, 2))
print(round(s2, 2))
print(round(theta_p, 2))
print(round(tmax, 2))

traps: Quoting τmax = R when σ1 and σ2 have the same sign. The zero stress then sits outside the pair and τabs = max(|σ1|,|σ2|)/2, which is bigger than R.
Giving 2θp instead of θp, or giving only one principal plane. The two planes are always 90° apart, and only substituting back tells you which carries σ1.
Sorting by size instead of by sign. With σx = −40 MPa and σy = −100 MPa both compressive, σ1 = −40 MPa is the algebraically larger even though it looks 'smaller'.
Using a wrong sign for τxy. Shear is positive on the +x face in the +y direction and positive on the +y face in the +x direction; a slip flips θp and nothing else.
Believing the principal plane has zero normal stress. Only the shear is zero; the normal stress there is C + R or C − R, usually not small.

quiz.q: Define a principal plane and a principal stress.
quiz.a: A principal plane is a plane through the point on which the shear stress is zero. The normal stress acting on it is a principal stress, and it is the largest or smallest normal stress at that point.

quiz.q: Why are the two principal planes always 90° apart?
quiz.a: The condition is tan2θp = 2τxy/(σx − σy). The tangent has period 180° in 2θp, so the two solutions of 2θp differ by 180°. Halving gives angles θp that differ by 90°.

quiz.q: A point has σx = 60 MPa, σy = 20 MPa, τxy = 0. Find σ1, σ2 and θp.
quiz.a: C = (60+20)/2 = 40 MPa, R = √(20² + 0) = 20 MPa. σ1 = 60 MPa, σ2 = 20 MPa. tan2θp = 0/40 = 0, so θp = 0° and 90°: the x and y faces are already principal planes.

quiz.q: A point has σx = 100 MPa, σy = 100 MPa, τxy = 40 MPa. Find the principal stresses, the maximum in-plane shear, the plane it acts on, and the absolute maximum shear.
quiz.a: C = 100 MPa, (σx − σy)/2 = 0, R = 40 MPa. σ1 = 140 MPa, σ2 = 60 MPa. tan2θp = 2(40)/0, so 2θp = 90° and θp = 45°; the maximum in-plane shear of 40 MPa acts on the x face (θs = 0°) and the y face (θs = 90°), which are 45° from the principal planes. For the absolute value, order the three principal stresses as 140, 60 and 0 MPa; the largest pair difference is 140 MPa, so τabs = 140/2 = 70 MPa, larger than R.

quiz.q: A shaft carries pure torsion, so σx = σy = 0 and τxy = τ. Find the principal stresses and the principal planes, and explain how a cast iron shaft fails.
quiz.a: C = 0, R = √(0 + τ²) = τ, so σ1 = +τ and σ2 = −τ. tan2θp = 2τ/0 → 2θp = 90°, θp = 45°. Cast iron is weak in tension, so it cracks on the plane of maximum tension, at 45° to the shaft axis, a helical break.

quiz.q: A point has σx = 80 MPa, σy = 20 MPa, τxy = −40 MPa. Find σ1 and σ2, and decide whether the in-plane maximum shear equals the absolute maximum shear.
quiz.a: C = 50 MPa, (σx − σy)/2 = 30 MPa, R = √(30² + 40²) = 50 MPa. σ1 = 100 MPa, σ2 = 0 MPa. In-plane τmax = 50 MPa. The zero stress also comes from the free surface, so the three principal stresses are 100, 0 and 0 MPa, and τabs = (100 − 0)/2 = 50 MPa. They are equal here.

beyond: Not for the exam. Principal stresses are what finite element software plots by default: a solver returns six stress components at each node, and post-processing diagonalises that 3×3 tensor to draw σ1 trajectories — the paths along which tension flows, used to place steel in concrete and fibres in composites. The same eigen-decomposition drives photoelasticity, where a loaded transparent model shows fringes at contours of (σ1 − σ2).
